claims.claim: An alleged optimum has a linear-time verifiable certificate, even for arbitrary signed entries.
claims.evidence: Let q=min(m,n). Checking all L-square sums costs at most mn prefix-sum queries, while checking one supplied violating square for every l>L costs at most q more. These conditions are sufficient because they prove L feasible and every larger length infeasible, and necessary because every length larger than the true optimum has a violating square. The L=0 case is correctly handled by witnesses for all positive lengths. Signed entries do not affect the exact prefix-sum identity. This is linear in unit-cost exact-word operations, the model used by the source's arithmetic bounds.
claims.witness: For a true optimum L, use one square of sum greater than k for every l in {L+1,...,q}; no feasibility witness beyond the exhaustive L-scan is needed.
claims.search_method: Direct soundness, completeness, and operation-count proof, supplemented by exhaustive exact-integer certificate checks.

claims.claim: There is an exact output-sensitive search algorithm whose worst-case time is O(mn min(m,n)).
claims.evidence: Descending examination returns the first feasible length, which is necessarily the maximum feasible length; each rejected larger length supplies the required certificate witness. For m>=n=q and l=q-t, there are exactly (m-n+t+1)(t+1) placements. Summing through d=q-L gives the stated O(mn+(m-n+1)(d+1)^2+(d+1)^3) bound. For L=0 the actual range ends at t=q-1, so including t=q is a valid upper bound. Since d<=q<=m, this is O(mnq), and constant d leaves O(mn).
claims.witness: Exhaustive checks compared descending search with brute-force maxima on 105,720 matrix/threshold cases and verified the placement bound and generated certificates.
claims.search_method: Direct descending-order correctness proof, exact summation of placement counts, and exhaustive small-instance comparison.

claims.claim: Feasibility can alternate at every side length, and the natural no-revisit greedy extension is incorrect.
claims.evidence: In the alternating-row construction, an even-length interval in the first row sums to zero. An odd-length interval sums to either 1 or -1, while a square excluding that row sums to zero, so F_l is exactly 0 for even l and 1 for odd l. At k=0 feasibility therefore changes at every consecutive length. In the 2-by-3 example, the side-2 sums are 1 and 4; after decreasing at the second placement, a no-revisit scan misses the earlier entry 2. Both lengths 2 and 1 are infeasible at k=1, so the correct output is 0 rather than 1.
claims.witness: k=0 with first row (1,-1,1,-1,...) and all other rows zero; separately k=1 with matrix [[2,1,1],[-3,1,1]].
claims.search_method: Closed-form interval-sum analysis plus exact evaluation through n=30, covering 465 side lengths, and direct evaluation of the greedy counterexample.

claims.claim: Any deterministic exact algorithm in the standard explicit one-word-per-entry cell-probe model requires Omega(mn) input probes in the worst case, even for Boolean matrices and k=0; thus an O(mn) algorithm would be optimal in this model.
claims.evidence: For q=min(m,n), top=min(r,m-q) and left=min(c,n-q) define an in-bounds q-square containing any selected cell (r,c). The all-zero input has answer q. If a cell unprobed on that execution is changed to one, the deterministic transcript remains identical, yet the covering q-square now has sum 1>0, making q infeasible. Hence every one of the mn input words must be probed on the zero input. This proves the claimed worst-case lower bound but correctly does not exclude O(mn).
claims.witness: The indistinguishable pair is the all-zero Boolean matrix and the matrix obtained by changing any purportedly unprobed cell to one, with k=0.
claims.search_method: Adaptive cell-probe adversary proof; the covering formula was also checked for all 3,025 cells in all shapes with 1<=m,n<=10.

claims.claim: The O(mn) endpoint is achievable for two nontrivial signed separable classes: multiplicative rank one and additive separability.
claims.evidence: For A_ij=u_i v_j, every l-square sum is a product of independently chosen vertical and horizontal window sums; the maximum of xy over two finite one-dimensional ranges occurs among the four endpoint products. The pivot identity pA_ij=A_icA_rj both recognizes rank at most one and makes every candidate (sum_i A_ic)(sum_j A_rj)/p an exact square sum. Evaluating all four quotients before maximizing handles p<0 correctly. For A_ij=u_i+v_j, the maximum is l(max X_l+max Y_l). Recognition identities are correct, and q(m+n)<=2mn establishes the runtime.
claims.witness: Exact enumeration covered 43,800 multiplicative and additive instances with factors in {-2,-1,0,1,2}, including zero factors and negative pivots.
claims.search_method: Algebraic factorization and extremum proof, recognition-identity verification, complexity derivation, and exhaustive exact-integer comparison with brute force.

claims.claim: If r rows and c columns are nonzero, there is an exact direct algorithm using O(mn+q min(rn,cm)) word operations; in particular, a constant number of nonzero rows or columns admits O(mn) time even with signed entries.
claims.evidence: For fixed l, supported row h belongs to precisely the vertical starts in [max(0,h-l+1),min(h,m-l)]. Its start and one-past-end form two monotone event lists. After grouped events at coordinate a are applied, each maintained T_b equals the corresponding l-square sum. Between event coordinates these values are unchanged, so scanning each realized state is exhaustive. Each of O(r) row events updates O(n) horizontal starts, giving O(rn) per length; the O(n) zero-state baseline is absorbed over all lengths by O(mn). Transposition yields O(cm) per length, and selecting the better orientation gives the stated bound. The initialization correctly distinguishes an empty zero state from a nonempty all-negative state.
claims.witness: Exact comparison with brute force passed on 32,889 matrices, including all {-1,0,1}-valued tested shapes and targeted empty-state, simultaneous-event, rectangular, and all-negative cases.
claims.search_method: Interval-membership proof, event-state invariant, operation count, transpose argument, and exhaustive exact-integer testing.

claims.claim: A thresholded max-plus-convolution scan embeds exactly into matrices supported on one row.
claims.evidence: For l=B-t and horizontal start s, telescoping gives window sum p_{B-(t-s)}-p_s. Writing i=s and j=t-s, a valid pair i,j<N yields C+x_i+y_j. If i>=N,j<N the sum is at most -1; if i<N,j>=N it is at most -C-1; and if both are invalid it is -2H. Valid sums are at least 1, while squares not containing the first row sum to zero. Therefore F_{B-t}=C+c_t exactly. Feasibility at threshold C+K is consequently equivalent to c_t<=K over the encoded high lengths, and the maximum feasible length identifies the least qualifying t.
claims.witness: The checker exhaustively tested 16,275 vector pairs and 80,025 encoded convolution coefficients for N<=3, along with thresholds from -5 through 5.
claims.search_method: Exact telescoping derivation, exhaustive invalid-index case split, threshold-decoding proof, and exact-integer enumeration.

claims.claim: Any single-matrix reduction that represents N distinct source indices by N distinct positive side lengths must create a matrix with at least N^2 explicit cells.
claims.evidence: An m-by-n instance has exactly q=min(m,n) positive square side lengths. Injectively assigning N source indices to distinct lengths forces q>=N. Both m and n are at least q, so mn>=q^2>=N^2. The draft properly limits this conclusion to the stated single-matrix, distinct-length template and draws no general hardness conclusion.
claims.witness: The symbolic chain is N<=q<=m,n, hence N^2<=q^2<=mn.
claims.search_method: Direct counting and dimension argument, supplemented by exact checks on 19,270 qualifying finite shapes.

claims.claim: If integer bit lengths are unbounded and bit operations are charged, an O(mn) bound independent of bit length is impossible.
claims.evidence: On a 1-by-1 instance, feasibility is the comparison a<=k. With a=k=2^(B-1), changing any one of the B-1 lower bits of a from zero to one produces a same-length input with a>k and the opposite answer. On the equality execution, an exact bit-access algorithm must therefore inspect every lower position; otherwise the corresponding altered input is indistinguishable. This gives Omega(B) bit cost. It is only an encoding-length obstruction and does not exclude O(mn) unit-cost word operations.
claims.witness: For each 0<=r<B-1, compare the equality input a=k=2^(B-1) with a=2^(B-1)+2^r and the same k.
claims.search_method: Deterministic decision-tree indistinguishability argument in the explicitly stated binary bit-cost model; no finite checker is needed for the asymptotic proof.

target_evidence: The draft does not provide an O(mn) algorithm for unrestricted signed matrices and does not prove that such an algorithm is impossible in the unit-cost bounded-word/arithmetic setting implicit in the source question. The Omega(mn) cell-probe bound merely matches the requested endpoint; the separable and sparse algorithms cover restricted classes; and the max-plus and dimension results identify structure without yielding an excluding lower bound. The unbounded-bit observation changes the cost parameter and is only the generic input-encoding obstruction, not a resolution of the source's substantive endpoint. The surviving results are nevertheless correct and material, so the proper target judgment is VALID_PARTIAL_PROGRESS, matching the draft's PARTIAL claim.
